results.title: Pure Java LP Solver Benchmark – oj! Algorithms
results.content: # Pure Java LP Solver Benchmark. ojAlgo contains pure Java LP, QP and MIP solvers. That, and the ojAlgo solver, are essentially the only alternatives. (There are some further alternatives mentioned at the end of this post.) This benchmark compares them to each other, and to the industry standard (native code) CPLEX solver. Each model-solver combination is evaluated multiple times – repeated until consecutive invocation times are stable within 1%. If a solver fails to find a correct solution for a particular model, no time is recorded. That model-solver pair is instead just marked as FAILED. In all cases the solvers are invoked via that model. That includes the ojAlgo solvers. Even within ojAlgo the model implementation and the various solver implementations are independent of each other. The ACM and CPLEX solver integrations are written by the ojAlgo developer. It should be pointed out that CPLEX is not just any native code solver. For the smallest/simplest models ojAlgo is actually faster than CPLEX (most likely related to overhead calling native code) but as size/complexity scales up CPLEX is clearly much faster. Also, ojAlgo fails to solve one of the models. (x-y scatter plot where the x-values are always CPLEX’s execution time for a particular model, and the y-values are ojAlgo’s or ACM’s execution times for the same model.) As can be seen in the chart there are fewer points for ACM than for ojAlgo. There are several native code (both Open Source and commercial) solver packages available with Java interfaces.

results.title: Benchmarking and tweaking | Using Timefold Solver | Timefold Solver 1.29.0 | Timefold Documentation
results.content: Luckily, Timefold Solver includes a benchmarker, which allows you to play out different solver phases with different settings against each other in development, so you can use the best configuration for your planning problem in production. The generated benchmark report already contains interesting information, but it doesn’t compare solver configurations to find the best algorithm. To quickly configure and run a benchmark for typical solver configs, use a `solverBenchmarkBluePrint` instead of `solverBenchmark`s:. Useful for visualizing trade-off between the best score versus the time spent for construction heuristics (presuming that no other solver phases are configured). To configure Matrix Benchmarking for Simulated Annealing (or any other configuration that involves a `Score` template variable), use the `replace()` method in the solver benchmark name element:. public File aggregateAllBenchmarks() { // Load benchmark configuration PlannerBenchmarkConfig benchmarkConfig = PlannerBenchmarkConfig.createFromXmlResource("benchmarkConfig.xml"); // Create and use the benchmark aggregator BenchmarkAggregator aggregator = new BenchmarkAggregator(); // Aggregate all benchmark results - returns HTML report file return aggregator.aggregateBenchmarks(benchmarkConfig); }.

Notifications You must be signed in to change notification settings. # alecjacobson/sparse-solver-benchmark. ## Folders and files. ## Repository files navigation. # 🚀 Sparse Positive Definite Linear System Solver Benchmark 📏. This is an informal benchmark for *k*-harmonic diffusion problems on triangle meshes found commonly in geometry processing. > * Eigen LLT/LDLT are **OK** but suffer for less sparse systems 🏅. > * catamari is **OK** for medium but inaccurate for big systems (bonus: it's MPL2 🆓). > * Eigen LU¹ is significantly **slower** 🐌. > ¹These systems are SPD so LU is not a good choice, but provides a reference. ## Build. mkdir build cd build cmake ../ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release make. ./sparse_solver_benchmark [path to triangle mesh]. ## What about this other solver XYZ? Please submit a pull request with a wrapper for solver XYZ. ## What are the systems being solved? This code will build a discretization of the ∆ᵏ operator and solve a system of the form:. where x is the surface's embedding. In matrix form this is:. (Wᵏ + M) u = M x. where Wᵏ is defined recursively as:. W¹ = L Wᵏ⁺¹ = Wᵏ M⁻¹ L. and `L` is the discrete Laplacian and `M` is the discrete mass matrix. This is a form of smoothing (k=1 is implicit mean curvature flow "Implicit Fairing of Irregular Meshes" Desbrun et al. 1999, k≥2 is higher order, e.g., "Mixed Finite Elements for Variational Surface Modeling" Jacobson et al. For k=1, the system is generally OK w.r.t. conditioning and the sparsity for a minifold mesh will be 7 non-zeros per row (on average). For k=3, the system can get really badly scaled and starts to become more dense (~40 non-zeros per row). No description, website, or topics provided. ### Stars. ### Forks. ## Releases.
